searchText: It's sort of indirect though, with the assumption that some subset of the stake is honest we still get that any misbehavior on a shard will be announced to the rest of the network and it won't be able to be finalized it's a weaker assumption but not very far removed Users can still validate as many shards as they wish to (AFAIK), just as users can validate as many L1s and L2s as they wish to (if their hardware + bandwidth is sufficient). Does splitting validators among committees (and shuffling around) reduce security a non-zero, negligible amount? (which approaches zero as committee sizes approach the total/original validator set) <@339771292884664320> the diagram in here is a pretty interesting way to think about it https://vitalik.ca/general/2020/08/20/trust.html the shard DAS is the bit that makes the shard chain custody trustworthy without relying on everyone in the network to have a copy of it sharded execution is a lot harder and is why it's not in the roadmap anymore Every full node does data availability sampling. This in combination with erasure encoding allowing reconstruction of the data allows for the network as a whole to be resistant to 99%+ vals making claims about unavailable data Many explanations of sharding only explain committee based custody which does assuming 2/3 val honesty but they fail to note that if committee based custody fails, they cannot trick the network to follow unavailable chains due to DAS You just gave me a few days of reading to understand this explanation thank you Damn what’s happening now is unreal Only because it has 0 users, a broken UI, and pool documentation. I actually tried to use it, but it appears to be just a prototype. I believe the team that built it is working on v2. This is the old form of sharding. what is the best way to do an ERC20 token airdrop to thousands of eth addresses (about 20k addresses) ? win the lottery because thats the only way your going to afford the gas... Join the Cryptodevs discord (link in <#745072678079168654> ). I'm not sure on the state of the art, but merkledrops are fairly popular: @transmissions11 (on twitter) has a library I believe.

excerpts.content: Every full node does data availability sampling. This in combination with erasure encoding allowing reconstruction of the data allows for the network as a whole to be resistant to 99%+ vals making claims about unavailable data
